summary: MPLS can load-balance flows using Entropy Labels, but an ingress router may only insert one if the egress has signalled it can process them. Knowing each router's Entropy Readable Label Depth is also useful. This document defines how to signal both capabilities using IS-IS and BGP-LS.

plainLanguage.summary: Delivery trucks can split loads between roads when each package has a random tag. This document tells routers how to announce they can handle those tags using IS-IS.

questions: what is entropy readable label depth
subtitle: How IS-IS routers announce whether they can handle entropy labels and how deep into a label stack they can read.

tldr.problem: An ingress MPLS router may not insert an entropy label unless the egress has signaled that it can process one, and it also helps to know how deep each router can read into the label stack.
tldr.mechanism: IS-IS carries the Entropy Label Capability in bit 3 of the Prefix Attribute Flags (the E-Flag) and the Entropy Readable Label Depth in a new MSD-Type, ERLD-MSD (type 2). Both can be passed on through BGP-LS.
tldr.outcome: Ingress routers learn, from the IGP, where entropy labels are safe to use and where to put them. Wrong values can cause poor load-balancing or dropped traffic.

today: RFC 9088 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Signal Entropy Labels in IS-IS
sections.content:
RFC 6790 describes how to load-balance MPLS traffic flows using Entropy Labels (EL). It also introduces the Entropy Label Capability (ELC) and defines how to signal it with MPLS signaling protocols. An ingress Label Switching Router (LSR) cannot insert ELs into packets for a given Label Switched Path unless the egress LSR has indicated that it can process them.

Labels can now also be signaled through link-state IGPs such as IS-IS (RFC 8667). This document therefore defines how to signal the ELC using IS-IS.

When Segment Routing is used with the MPLS data plane (SR-MPLS, RFC 8660), ingress LSRs also benefit from knowing each router's Entropy Readable Label Depth (ERLD), defined in RFC 8662. It helps them find where the EL belongs in the stack, and whether several ELs at different positions are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can spread traffic over many paths if packets carry a random tag. Before using the tag, the sender needs to know the receiver understands it, so this document defines a way to announce that.

sections.title: Advertising ELC: The E-Flag
sections.content:
ELC is really a property of a node, but the RFC explains that it is often handy to attach it to a prefix. In a multi-area or multi-domain network, an ingress router may not know who originated a remote prefix or what that originator can do.

The signal is bit 3 of the Prefix Attribute Flags (RFC 7794), used as the ELC Flag, or E-Flag. It is set on a local host prefix of the originating node when the node supports ELC on all interfaces.

  • A router with several interfaces MUST NOT announce ELC for local host prefixes unless all of its interfaces can process ELs.
  • If all interfaces can, it SHOULD set ELC on every local host prefix it advertises in IS-IS.
  • ELC signaling MUST be preserved when a router propagates a prefix between IS-IS levels (RFC 5302).
  • When redistributing a prefix between IS-IS instances, or from another protocol into IS-IS, a router SHOULD preserve the ELC signaling if it exists. How ELC is exchanged between protocol instances on an Autonomous System Border Router is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A router raises a small flag saying it understands the random tags, but only if every one of its doors can handle them. The flag must stay raised as the news passes along.

sections.title: Advertising ERLD: The ERLD-MSD
sections.content:
To advertise a router's ERLD, the RFC defines a new MSD-Type (RFC 8491) called ERLD-MSD. IANA assigned MSD-Type code 2 to it. The MSD-Value field carries the ERLD, in the range 0 to 255, and the scope of the advertisement depends on the application.

If a router has several interfaces with different abilities to read the label stack, it MUST advertise the smallest value found across all of them.

The absence of an ERLD-MSD advertisement only means that the node does not support advertising this capability. It says nothing about the actual depth. If ERLD-MSD shows up in the Link MSD sub-TLV, it MUST be ignored. Other considerations for advertising ERLD are in RFC 8662.
sections.plainLanguage: The router also tells others how many labels deep it can peek into a stack. If its doors differ, it reports the smallest number so nobody is let down.

sections.title: Carrying the Signals in BGP-LS
sections.content:
The IS-IS extensions can be advertised through BGP-LS (RFC 7752), which distributes link-state and traffic engineering information using BGP, by reusing existing BGP-LS TLVs. No new BGP-LS TLVs are defined.

  • The ELC is advertised using the Prefix Attribute Flags TLV, as defined in RFC 9085.
  • The ERLD-MSD is advertised using the Node MSD TLV, as defined in RFC 8814.
sections.plainLanguage: The same news can be passed to far-away systems using an existing message system, with no new kind of message needed.

sections.title: IANA Registry Entries
sections.content: IANA completed two actions. Bit 3 in the "Bit Values for Prefix Attribute Flags Sub-TLV" registry was assigned to the ELC Flag, and the registry was updated to use the name ELC Flag (E-Flag). Type 2 in the "IGP MSD-Types" registry was assigned to the ERLD-MSD, and the registry was updated to use the name ERLD-MSD.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers now records which flag and which type number mean these two announcements.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document adds node capabilities to IS-IS and BGP-LS, so the security considerations of RFC 7752, RFC 7794, RFC 7981, RFC 8491, RFC 8662, RFC 8814 and RFC 9085 apply.

Incorrectly setting the E-Flag during origination, propagation or redistribution may lead to poor or no load-balancing of MPLS traffic, or to MPLS traffic being discarded on the egress node. Incorrectly setting the ERLD value may lead to poor or no load-balancing.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router raises the flag by mistake, packets may be spread badly or thrown away. A wrong depth number also hurts the spreading.
